item.title: Trump says he's weighing deal with Iran against action to "finish them off"
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the U.S. would not change his country's positions, after President Trump said Washington "may do another little Epic Fury."Iran warned on Saturday that U.S. ships would never be allowed in the Persian Gulf "under any circumstances," as tensions between Tehran and Washington continue mounting. Both sides have signaled a possible return to strikes, with the U.S. ambassador to Turkey warning Iran could be struck as soon as this weekend.Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.

Houthis say they launched attacks on Riyadh airport, hours after reopening
A spokesperson for Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said they launched attacks on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, just hours after it resumed flights. Deadly strikes by the rebel group earlier this month had forced the airport to shut down operations for more than two weeks.
"The Yemeni armed forces conducted three military operations with dozens of ballistic missiles," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on X, saying the strike on the airport "achieved its target." He said additional strikes targeted King Khalid air base in Khamis Mushait and a naval base in Jazan.
Saree previously warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target," as the airport prepared to resume international flights.

item.title: Venezuela opposition leader María Corina Machado returns to country
item.description:
Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel laureate María Corina Machado is back in her home country after nearly a year in exile, her team confirmed to CBS News on Sunday.
"I am here. With you," Machado posted in Spanish on X.
She did not disclose more details about her current location or how she returned.
Machado's senior adviser David Smoalnsky said in a statement to CBS that her return is "a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections in the near future."
"Machado returns to stand with Venezuelans in their pursuit of freedom, democracy, and justice, and to help advance a peaceful, inclusive, and sustainable transition leading to free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections, with guarantees for all," he said, thanking President Trump, the U.S. government and others for "their continued leadership and support."
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado greets supporters at a church in Barquisimeto, Venezuela, on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026.
Vente Venezuela Press Office via AP
Machado covertly snuck out of the South American country in December with a private U.S. rescue team to accept the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, her first public appearance in 11 months. The event was a month before the U.S. military deposed the country's then-President Nicolás Maduro.
Machado, who was barred by Maduro's government from exiting Venezuela, is considered a fugitive by the Venezuelan government, which accuses her of calling for military intervention against the country.
Edmundo Gonzalez, a former presidential candidate for Machado's movement who has been living in Spain, confirmed her return in his own social media post and said he would be next to her "very soon."

item.title: Transcript: Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 25, 2026
item.description:
The following is the transcript of the interview with Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 25, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to the Texas governor's race and Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa. She joins us from Austin. Good to have you here.
TEXAS STATE REPRESENTATIVE GINA HINOJOSA: It's great to be with you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, if you win, you would be the first Democratic governor and the first female governor in over 30 years. You're running in a state, though, that has more Republicans than Democrats. So, what is your message to get Republicans to cross over and vote for you?
HINOJOSA: Well, right now, nobody wants politics as usual. Most of us see that it is broken, and so what we are seeing in Texas is because there is deep disappointment in both political parties, people are forging a new way for- forward. One that is postpartisan in some ways. The data centers are a physical manifestation of a governor, Governor Abbott, and a government that's working for the moneyed interests and leaving the people of Texas to fend for themselves. Public schools are another issue where there has been a bipartisan coming together in support of our public schools. And so, listen, this creates an opportunity for Texans to evaluate the candidate. I believe that's why we have now six or seven polls out of the last six weeks that show us winning. All polls show us within the margin of error. Turnout is high. Enthusiasm is high on our side, so we feel really good about where we are.

item.title: Transcript: Sen. Thom Tillis on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 25, 2026
item.description:
The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 25, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to North Carolina Republican Senator Tom Tillis, who joins us from Charlotte this morning. Good morning to you, sir.
SENATOR THOM TILLIS: Good morning.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I want to ask you to be a bit of a pundit before we get into some policy. CBS polling shows voters see corruption as a major factor, 83% see it as a concern in determining their vote, and they see it as more of an issue with Republicans. How does your party overcome this perception?
SEN. TILLIS: Well, I think a part of what we have to do is be open about what we've done right and where we've kind of skated into the gray area. I'll give you a good example of why I think maybe people feel that way. You can't have an oligarch pay tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars for the president's son's wedding and not make it look odd, particularly when that oligarch is aligned with Putin and has gone on delegations with Putin to Beijing. That's just one example. What we need to do is learn the rule of figure out where the line is and take a step back, or American people are already predisposed to assume Democrats and Republicans are corrupt. We're just feeding that narrative when we let things like that happen, whether it's legal or not. It's irrelevant.

item.title: Transcript: Rep. Jason Crow on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 25, 2026
item.description:
The following is the transcript of the interview with Rep. Jason Crow, Democrat of Colorado, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Oct. 25, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: We go now to Democratic Congressman Jason Crow of Colorado, who is in Denver this morning. Congressman, our CBS polling shows Democrats are on pace to have a narrow majority of about 11 seats and that for most voters who are backing Democrats, they tell us their motivation is more about stopping Trump and GOP policies than advancing other policies. Is that how you think your party will govern the House in opposition?
REPRESENTATIVE JASON CROW: You know- you know politics is really interesting. There's a lot of weird things about politics in this job. But one of the weird things is when, you know, the political class comes out with polling and they're like, "Hey, Americans want to be able to pay their bills and afford health care and afford housing and- and groceries." I mean, that- that's just it always has been true, always will be true. It always will be the primary thing people are concerned about. It's actually what we're running on. As the battleground chair for House Democrats, I have recruited and mentored this battlefield of candidates. It's what they're running on, it's what we're going to win on, and it's what we're going to address when we get into power in January.

item.title: Israel to close West Bank crossings before elections amid military operation
item.description:
The Israeli military continued a massive operation in the occupied West Bank on Sunday, placing major restrictions on movement ahead of Israel's upcoming elections.
The operation, which comes in response to a gun attack that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others in Hebron on Friday, has displaced hundreds of Palestinians over the last two days.
In Hebron, more than 2,200 people, including nearly 200 children under the age of 18, have been displaced, the municipality said. Since Friday's attack, all entrances and exits to the city have remained sealed, with the epicenter of the operation in Deir Bahha and another part of the city called Al-Jalda, according to Hebron Mayor Yousef Zuhair Al-Jabari.
"People cannot reach or enter the city, and they cannot leave it. The blockade has affected every aspect of life," Al-Jabari said.
Israeli military operations continue as Israeli soldiers raid numerous homes and prevent members of the press from covering the operations in Hebron, West Bank, Palestine, on Oct. 25, 2026.
Mamoun Wazwaz/Anadolu via Getty Images
The Israeli military said it operated in more than 400 different locations over the weekend and arrested 40 Palestinians it claimed were affiliated with Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad.
Additionally, the Israeli military said most Palestinian workers with permits will not be allowed to enter Israeli settlements for work on Sunday and Monday, and crossings into Israel will remain closed until after Tuesday's Israeli elections.
The election is largely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership and security policies during the past three years of war.
